articles.title_orig: Chinese AI lab Moonshot turned to Europe for Nvidia Blackwell access amid U.S. China curbs, sources tell CNBC
articles.title_zh: Chinese AI lab Moonshot turned to Europe for Nvidia Blackwell access amid U.S. China curbs, sources tell CNBC
articles.content_orig:
Moonshot AI, a Chinese artificial intelligence lab that the White House accused of accessing Nvidia advanced chips remotely in East Asia, has sought access to the chips through data centers in Europe, sources have told CNBC.
Deals have been discussed this year for Moonshot to rent capacity from neoclouds hosting Nvidia graphics processing units, or GPUs, at facilities in Europe, four people familiar with the matter said. They asked not to be named because they were discussing private information.
Nvidia's effective monopoly over the most powerful chips has made U.S. export controls a key tool in Washington's effort to preserve its advantage over China in the AI race. American AI labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic are locked in a training and pricing battle with Chinese developers, including Moonshot AI, which makes the Kimi family of models.
Moonshot was looking to lease capacity powered by Nvidia's Blackwell systems, advanced chips currently subject to those export controls which effectively ban their import into China, three of the sources told CNBC.
In July, the White House said the Chinese AI lab had accessed Nvidia's Blackwell chips via a facility in Thailand.
U.S. export controls restrict the shipment of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China, but remote access via overseas data centers offers a loophole. Current law does not give regulators broad authority to control companies' access to those chips through cloud services hosted overseas.
Moonshot, Nvidia, the White House, the U.S. Department of Commerce, China's embassy in the U.K. and its Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not respond to a request for comment.
Chinese developers have made notable capability gains in the past six months and greater access to Nvidia chips could put even more pressure on their American rivals.
To lease Nvidia computing power in Europe, a Chinese AI company would typically rent capacity from a non-Chinese neocloud or data center operator that can purchase advanced chips.
Moonshot was interested in leasing capacity on clusters for inference, which refers to serving models to end users, in Europe, two of the sources said. One of the sources said they were also aware of interest in clusters for training.
Talks for arrangements that would see Moonshot rent access to clusters of 8,000 or more Blackwell GPUs hosted in the region have taken place, one source said. They described the Chinese AI lab as "very aggressive" in its pursuit of more computing power.
One of the sources told CNBC that talks on securing Moonshot compute in Europe had taken place since the White House said it had done so via Thailand. Moonshot did not comment at the time.
Founded in 2023, Beijing-based Moonshot AI is one of China's leading model builders. It released a new model in July that Moonshot said closed the gap with leading systems built by Anthropic and OpenAI.
The model saw significant uptake as a cheaper alternative to U.S. offerings. Chinese AI models have surged in global adoption in 2026 , amid capability gains and lower costs than U.S. rivals.
Around the time Kimi K3 was released, Moonshot said demand had stretched its capacity, and it temporarily paused new subscriptions to prioritize compute for current members. "We're adding capacity as fast as we can and will reopen new subscription spots in batches," the company said in a LinkedIn post.
Leasing AI compute is a booming industry, with customers, or offtakers, typically taking capacity for a fee and paying an upfront cost to secure the deal, which is a percentage of the lifetime contract value.
One source said it had been proposed that Moonshot pay 30% to 50% more upfront than a non-Chinese offtaker would.
Arrangements with Chinese customers can be more lucrative upfront, as neoclouds and financing firms look to hedge against a potential future ban of remote access agreements.
In Washington, lawmakers have proposed the Remote Access Security Act (RASA) to expand U.S. export controls to include the cloud-based access of critical hardware and software. It passed the House of Representatives in January but has not passed the Senate.
The Financial Times reported on Tuesday that the chip giant told cloud providers selling access to their chips that they must sell at least 51% of services to non-Chinese customers.
Asked about the reports earlier this week, an Nvidia spokesperson said: "America cannot win the AI race unless America's AI infrastructure wins worldwide — if the world's clouds rely on foreign-made chips, the model and application layers will be foreign-built as well."
Nvidia said in August that Washington had licensed some sales of its H200 AI chips, an older generation, but that "such sales were restricted" by the Chinese government, which has sought to boost domestic chipmakers by limiting access to Nvidia chips.

articles.title_orig: 'Too early' to say if Europe flight bomb threats linked, EU says
articles.title_zh: 'Too early' to say if Europe flight bomb threats linked, EU says
articles.content_orig:
The EU said on Thursday it was not yet clear whether a spate of hoax bomb alerts targeting European flights were connected and that it was following events closely with national authorities.
"Any threats against civilians are unacceptable," EU transport commissioner Apostolos Tzitzikostas posted on X, adding that it was "too early to draw conclusions on whether the reported incidents are linked."
The statement from Brussels comes after Italian, French and Bulgarian fighter jets scrambled as at least 14 European flights were hit by hoax bomb alerts for the third day this week, authorities and airlines said.
The hoaxes particularly targeted low-cost carriers and flights to or from Bulgaria, Czech Republic and Italy.
Italian air force jets escorted a Finnair flight from Helsinki to Rome while French fighters guided a Aer Lingus Dublin-Rome flight to a military base outside Paris. Bulgaria's air force escorted three planes targeted by threats.
Three flights were diverted in all but all the jets landed safely with no explosives found.
More than 20 hoaxes have now been reported this week with low-cost carrier Ryanair the victim of at least seven.
Three Ryanair planes headed for Sofia from Madrid, Copenhagen, and London Stansted were targeted by bomb threats, a spokesperson for the Bulgarian Ministry of Transport said.
Two of the planes landed in Sofia but the flight from London-Stansted was diverted to Plovdiv Airport, east of the capital.
Air force fighter jets escorted all three planes, the defence ministry said, saying such missions "detect, identify and escort the aircraft."
All three planes were later inspected, and no explosives were found, an interior ministry spokesperson told the AFP news agency.
A Finnair flight from Helsinki to Rome was escorted to Rome by a fighter jet and checked by bomb experts, a Rome Fiumicino Airport spokesperson told AFP.
A Finnair spokesperson Stiina Tuunanen, confirmed that "nothing unusual was found" when the jet landed.
Finnair has a “very clear process that we follow in situations like this and we always work closely with the local authorities," Tuunanen said.
She said another false bomb threat had targeted flight AY1471 from Helsinki to Vienna, without providing further information.
After receiving a threat, a Wizz Air flight from Milan to Warsaw was re-routed to Vienna, the airline said, "in accordance with established safety protocols and procedures".
Another Wizz Air flight from Milan to Bucharest landed at its destination safely, "following which a crisis unit was set up at Henri Coanda Airport," the Romanian intelligence service said in a statement.
An Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome was rerouted to France after a bomb threat. It was escorted by military aircraft to the Evreux air base west of Paris, French authorities said.
"The flight landed safely and Aer Lingus will work to reaccommodate customers to their final destination as soon as possible,” the airline said in a statement.
Four Prague-bound planes flown by Ryanair, Easy Jet and Sky Express were also the target of threats.
"We perceive the credibility of the threats as low," said Czech police on X. "Nevertheless, we are not underestimating the situation and all necessary security measures have been activated."
Prague Airport spokeswoman Denisa Hejtmankova told AFP the airport had received all the threats in emails from anonymous addresses. It was not immediately clear which airlines were involved.
Two planes, meanwhile, that arrived at Copenhagen were also the object of threats.
"Our assessment is that there is no danger, and there has never been any danger, to passengers or anyone else at the airport," Copenhagen police told AFP.
The origin and motives of the threats were unknown, but come amid a rise in hybrid attacks in Europe, sometimes linked by authorities to Russia or Iran.
France's secretary general for defence and national security, Nicolas Roche, highlighted to parliament last month "the massing of hybrid attacks in all their diversity — sabotage, cyber, drones, espionage of course —that we are seeing take shape in Europe."
On Tuesday, 10 flights were targeted with bomb threats, all of which turned out to be hoaxes.
The alerts forced the closure of a Warsaw airport and the deployment of Italian air force jets to protect flights.
On Monday, a Wizz Air flight from London's Luton airport to Sofia was diverted due a bomb threat and forced to make an emergency stop in Budapest.

articles.title_orig: Wendy’s Rejects Trian’s $1.4 Billion Takeover Offer
articles.title_zh: Wendy’s Rejects Trian’s $1.4 Billion Takeover Offer
articles.content_orig:
Wendy's on Thursday said that it is rejecting a $1.4 billion takeover offer from a group of investors led by Nelson Peltz's Trian Fund Management.
The group offered $7.35 per share in cash on Oct. 28 to take the struggling burger chain private . In addition to Trian, it included investment firms BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners, plus Flynn Group, one of Wendy's largest franchisees.
In February, Wendy's board formed a committee of independent directors to assess any potential bid from Trian in response to a regulatory filing from the firm. The committee found that the proposal "substantially undervalues" Wendy's and does not reflect potential gains from the chain's ongoing turnaround strategy, the company said in a press release on Thursday.
"Our confidence rests firmly in [CEO] Bob Wright's proven track record of seasoned industry leadership, including restaurant business turnarounds," Art Winkleblack, Wendy's board chair and a member of the independent committee, said in a statement.
Trian declined to comment on Wendy's decision.
To stave off a hostile takeover, Wendy's has adopted a shareholder rights plan — or poison pill — with a one-year duration, as of Wednesday, the company said. Wendy's added that the investor group led by Trian rejected an offer from Wendy's for a standstill agreement that would have paused additional share purchases, adding to Wendy's decision to use a poison pill.
The rejection is the latest in the long-running saga between Peltz and the burger chain, which dates back to an activist campaign he led more than two decades ago. A Peltz firm has even owned Wendy's before. In 2008, his company Triarc, which also owned Arby's, bought Wendy's in a $2.3 billion deal. It later sold Arby's, turning Wendy's into a standalone company again.
In 2024, Wendy's named Peltz as chairman emeritus after he spent 17 years on the company's board. Trian executive Peter May and Peltz's son, Bradley, still sit on Wendy's board.
Wendy's also reported its third-quarter results on Thursday. Its same-store sales declined for the seventh straight quarter. However, its quarterly earnings and revenue topped Wall Street's expectations.
Shares of Wendy's fell less than 1% in premarket trading. The takeover offer had lifted the stock, which has lost about 60% of its value over the last three years.
Wendy's is not the only restaurant chain that has found itself in the crosshairs of activist investors recently. Applebee's owner Dine Brands recently adopted a poison pill to block a takeover bid from investment firms Arkhouse Management and Cobblers Cove Capital.

articles.title_orig: Three ways the interest rate rise could affect you
articles.title_zh: Three ways the interest rate rise could affect you
articles.content_orig:
Interest rates have been raised for the first time in more than three years - and it could be good and bad news for you.
Here are three ways the increase to 4% from 3.75% could affect you.
Rate-setters at the Bank make changes to interest rates to fulfil their role of keeping price rises at a steady level.
Higher rates are meant to encourage people to spend less, reducing demand for goods and services and limiting price rises.
This impacts businesses in two ways - less money to spend among their customers may mean they sell less, but also the cost of borrowing to invest as a company goes up.
Many businesses, particularly small ones, have variable rate loans which are influenced by the Bank rate.
Firms say higher rates limit their ability to offer new jobs and wage rises.
Mitchell Barnes, founder and chief executive of Ryse 3D, which manufactures 3D parts for the defence and automotive sectors, said the "reality" of rising interest rates was to look at the cost of employees and people.
That could include greater use of robots rather than workers.
"It's going to cause issues with, I suppose, employment across all sectors for people," he said.
"You're going to see reduced employment, more automation, more robotics being put into facilities, just in order to increase efficiency and make that money go further."
The Bank rate - and where it is expected to go in future - has a significant impact on the interest rates customers are offered on savings products.
So, if you're saving up for something quite expensive, like a holiday, or very expensive, like a home, then a rate rise could be good news.
When interest rates were low throughout the 2010s, the returns for savers were poor, but borrowing costs were low too.
The answer then and now, according to experts, is to make sure you move your savings to benefit from the best possible rates.
Leaving your savings in an old account (a product not offered to new customers), rather than shopping around, can mean you are penalised for your loyalty.
"Savers have endured years of unrewarded loyalty, with those leaving [a £20,000 cash pot] in closed accounts losing out on an extra £139 over the past three years compared to on-sale easy access accounts," said Rachel Springall, from financial information service Moneyfacts.
She also said locking away your money for longer, with a fixed-term deal, is usually more lucrative.
The other flipside is that renting while you save could get more expensive, because a rising Bank rate may well increase costs for landlords.
The big losers from a rate rise are those who borrow money, and specifically those on variable rate mortgages.
About 500,000 homeowners have a mortgage that "tracks" the Bank of England's rate.
Any rise in the Bank rate means an increase in the monthly repayments on their outstanding loan. For a typical loan, the cost is going up by about £31 a month now the Bank has raised the base rate, but it depends on the size of people's loans.
An additional 500,000 homeowners on standard variable rates (SVRs) must wait to see if their lender chooses to pass on any Bank rate rise. Typically, this would mean a £14 increase per month in repayments for a 0.25 percentage points rates rise.
If you, like 87% of mortgage-holders, have a fixed-rate deal, then the payments will stay the same until the end of your current deal, which is usually two or five years.
While monthly payments are not immediately affected by a rate change, future deals are. Lenders had already "priced in" the latest rate rise when quoting new deals. Expectations for the Bank rate into next year are crucial on what they offer next.
The average rate on fixed deals are much higher now than was predicted at the start of the year. It means those remortgaging, possibly after the post-Covid boom in the housing market, are facing the prospect of higher mortgage payments.
Some people have been choosing to move onto tracker deals instead, taking a view -  including some risk - of the Bank rate not moving towards a series of further hikes.

articles.title_orig: Putin will not be invited to Britain's G20 summit, UK PM Burnham says
articles.title_zh: Putin will not be invited to Britain's G20 summit, UK PM Burnham says
articles.content_orig:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said Vladimir Putin is not invited to the G20 summit in Manchester.
Asked whether the Russian president would be invited to the annual meeting, which the UK is hosting in November 2027, Burnham said "no" because of sanctions against the Kremlin.
The UK has a longstanding policy not to have direct, bilateral engagement with Russian ministers since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.
But US president Donald Trump has sparked controversy by inviting Putin to this year's G20, which he will host in Miami in December. The Kremlin has not yet said whether Putin will attend.
Russia is a member of the G20 - a group of 19 nations, the European Union and African Union - while Ukraine is not, but the ongoing war in Ukraine has loomed large over recent summits.
Putin has not attended any major global summit since he launched his invasion and ongoing war in Ukraine.
Asked about inviting him to the G20 in Manchester in 2027, Burnham told The Economist he "will not be coming because of an outstanding sanction" on senior Russian figures.
He said the meeting would provide "a real opportunity" to work with Chinese president Xi Jinping on safety regulations for artificial intelligence (AI).
Pressed on whether the UK could bring the US and China around the same table to agree on global AI supervision, Burnham said: "As I sit here today, that feels challenging, but we've got to hold out the need to find global agreements on AI.
"If we don't, the risks of recent times will magnify, they will significantly intensify.
"So you've got to go into it with that aim."
He stressed the need "to find global agreements on AI," adding: "If we don't, the risks of recent times will magnify, they will significantly intensify. So you've got to go into it with that aim."
His decision not to include Putin in next year's gathering in Manchester comes after European diplomats refused to stand for an official photo with Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov at the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting in October.
The so-called "family photo" would usually include representatives from all nations in attendance, but this year it was cancelled.
The US decision to invite Lavrov in the first place - which itself came after further public rows between Trump and Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky - also attracted criticism.
Discussing Ukraine, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband later told Lavrov at the summit: "Let me say this directly to the Russian foreign minister: We all know who the aggressor in this war is."
The UK last hosted the G20 summit in 2009. Next year's two-day event will take place in the Manchester Central Convention Centre in Manchester city centre and host thousands of diplomats and delegates, as well as world leaders.
The government has said it will use its G20 presidency in 2027 to "reinforce global economic stability" and "benefit people in every part of the UK".

articles.title_orig: Discord is ditching Electron and its new app uses less RAM
articles.title_zh: Discord is ditching Electron and its new app uses less RAM
articles.content_orig:
Discord is moving its apps fully over to the Rust programming language.
Discord is moving its apps fully over to the Rust programming language.
Discord is finally giving up on Electron, the cross-platform framework that lets developers build desktop apps using web technologies. Electron web apps are notoriously heavy on system resources, and Discord is now moving its desktop app fully to Rust — a modern programming language designed for speed and memory safety.
“We’ve been early adopters of Rust since 2018 and a lot of our infra, voice tech, and even some of the current client is already Rust, the holy grail was getting the whole client there,” explains Discord chief technology officer Stanislav Vishnevskiy in a post on X . “That means Electron goes away, and so does React Native, mobile keeps native UI but shares app code with desktop via Rust.”
Vishnevskiy also shared an image of the Discord Windows client using just 290MB of RAM, which is a clear improvement as you only have to participate in a few servers and RAM usage can easily hit 1GB or more using the current Windows app.
It’s not clear when Discord will make the full switch over to Rust, but Vishnevskiy says the company “hope to get it into testing with users soon.”

articles.title_orig: China threatens retaliation as EU mulls trade “kill-switch”
articles.title_zh: China threatens retaliation as EU mulls trade “kill-switch”
articles.content_orig:
China’s ambassador to the EU, Cai Run, threatened on Thursday to retaliate if the EU adopted unilateral measures against Chinese interests.
The statement came as the European Commission is working on a new trade defence tool, dubbed a “kill-switch,” that could cut off Chinese access to the EU market in the event of serious market disruption caused by its aggressive trade policies.
“China opposes politicising economic and trade issues, overstretching the concept of security, and resorting to unilateral or maximum pressure,” Cai said.
He added: “If the EU side insists on adopting restrictive and discriminatory measures against China, China will have to take countermeasures to firmly safeguard its interests.”
As the EU faces a record-high trade deficit with China of €1 billion a day, Brussels is seeking to protect its market from low-cost Chinese imports, which have surged by 25% over the past year, according to Chinese customs.
Last October, EU leaders tasked the European Commission with developing an instrument that could be rapidly deployed against countries whose political or economic actions have serious repercussions for the EU market.
EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič told MEPs on Wednesday that the tool should be presented by the end of the year and would allow the EU “to react much faster, even by limiting the exports into the European Union.” He added that it would target “countries which are treating us [the EU] unfairly or which are harming European interests.”
Presented as country-agnostic, the tool would nevertheless directly target Chinese interests, which rely heavily on the EU’s 450 million consumers to sell their excess of production.
France and Germany pushed for such an instrument in early October, as every EU member state now faces a trade deficit with Beijing, with Chinese imports threatening entire sectors of their industries.
The Franco-German move came amid ongoing negotiations between Brussels and Beijing, which had begun the previous June with the aim of rebalancing trade relations. It also came just days before the Commission reached a deal on 9 October to reduce Chinese imports of hybrid cars into the EU.
Since the deal on cars, talks have resumed at a technical level between EU and Chinese officials, with Brussels hoping to replicate such an agreement in other sectors. A new meeting between Šefčovič and China’s Commerce Minister Wang Wentao is scheduled for March 2027.
Given the urgency of the situation, EU leaders have also asked the Commission to adopt measures, including quotas and tariffs, against Chinese imports in the chemicals and machinery industries, as pressure on the EU market has become unsustainable for European producers.
Šefčovič has repeatedly said that, with thousands of jobs at stake in the EU, the EU-China trade issue had become a political one in Europe, with high expectations among EU citizens.
Despite ongoing talks with China since June, the Commission has continued to impose additional duties on Chinese imports entering the EU following investigations product by product that found Chinese producers were benefiting from unfair pricing or subsidies from China.
This is not the first time China has threatened the EU with countermeasures. It already did so against a bill – the Industrial Accelerator Act - currently under discussion by the EU’s co-legislators seeking to limit access to EU public procurement and impose strict conditions on investments in the EU market, also targeting Beijing without explicitly naming it.

articles.title_orig: America got the anti-data-center wave it voted for. Here come the economic consequences
articles.title_zh: America got the anti-data-center wave it voted for. Here come the economic consequences
articles.content_orig:
A stunning upset in the Texas governor race and sweeping Democratic victories across the country threaten to curtail the biggest-ever spending boom in US history.
That could disrupt a key growth engine for America’s economy .
Come January, states controlled by Democrats who support expanding or extending AI construction moratoriums will account for 45% of America’s planned data center capacity, according to Goldman Sachs. A quarter of America’s planned AI infrastructure buildout is set to take place in Texas alone.
That doesn’t mean half of America’s planned data centers are on hold. Demand for AI is off the charts. Donald Trump is still president, and he’s already waving around his veto hat. And Democratic governors couldn’t stop every data center from being constructed even if they wanted to.
But Tuesday’s election nevertheless represents a paradigm shift that could alter the pace and path of America’s nonstop AI spending spree – an investment boom that has, according to ING economists, accounted for as much as a quarter of total US economic growth this year.
Those economic benefits are already real, supporting thousands of jobs. And AI has the potential to revolutionize the way we work.
But an AI data center slowdown could come with important silver linings. It could rein in unfettered growth that has contributed to rebounding inflation and led to widespread public antipathy toward the technology and the data centers that house it. It could also curtail some questionable business models that have raised serious skepticism on Wall Street.
Tapping the brakes could ultimately put AI – and the US economy – on a more sustainable path.
AI infrastructure spending is expected to approach $1 trillion a year, every year, for the foreseeable future, according to Columbia Business School economist Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh. As a percentage of America’s gross domestic product, that would outpace every other investment boom in modern US history – including the construction of the railroads.
The outcome of Tuesday’s elections could slow that spending, with vast consequences for the thousands of jobs and massive amounts of economic development that AI supports.
Democrats gained gubernatorial seats in Nevada, Georgia, Ohio and Texas, where candidates campaigned on tightening data center regulations. Proposals from the governors-elect include ending tax breaks, tightening climate and electricity restrictions and allowing local governments to impose their own moratoriums on data center construction.
But Texas is the big kahuna. Wells Fargo estimates that for every 10% reduction in planned Texas data center capacity, Big Tech companies will reduce their AI infrastructure spending by a stunning 1.6% (a lot of money when you’re measuring spending in the trillions of dollars).
State and local politicians have a lot of jurisdiction and sway over that spending: enough to change whether some projects get financed, said Mona Dajani, co-chair of Cooley’s infrastructure, energy and real estate practice.
Hundreds of data center developments that are still awaiting permits, utility service or tax incentives could be particularly exposed, Dajani noted. But even active construction projects could be threatened. Texas law grandfathers in some projects’ permits, protecting them from future changes to local permitting requirements – but that doesn’t resolve state permitting changes or electrical service guarantees that Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa could vacate.
The wait for approvals could add significant costs for AI companies, Dajani said: Interest, equipment commitments and utility expenses will all continue to accrue, even while a project is on ice. At some point, existing projects could stop being financially viable.
If that happens, AI companies – who have already strained to build out data centers fast enough to meet their anticipated demand – may not be able to meet their explosive spending targets.
“This is a rare case where state and local leaders have influence of geopolitical-level import,” said Harry Krejsa, director of studies at the Carnegie Mellon Institute for Strategy & Technology.
Data centers aren’t exclusively a Democratic issue: Americans have displayed bipartisan consensus for putting guardrails around data center buildouts.
Texas Republican Governor Greg Abbott had already imposed a data center moratorium that Hinojosa campaigned on extending until lawmakers establish stronger AI regulations.
But Trump had railed against any attempts to stymie AI’s growth and spending, citing economic and national security – particularly in the high-stakes race against China. Many Republican politicians who may have otherwise supported AI regulations, including frameworks for data center construction, remained silent.
Still, there’s evidence that the AI buildout could be on an unsustainable path.
The United States had 5,427 data centers at the end of last year, according to Stanford University’s AI Index Report , and AI companies have announced plans for 3,969 new US data centers, according to Aterio , a data center research company. But only about 800 are under construction, and AI experts have raised doubts about the viability of many of the announced projects.
If Tuesday’s election results trigger an investment slowdown, that could trim some of the industry’s fat.
Example A: CoreWeave, a neocloud business that rents out computing capacity, recently projected such extensive losses that its bond yields surged to 15% – the danger zone. That was particularly troubling, because its expected return on investment was only around 9%.
In other words, CoreWeave loses money on every single dollar it spends on expanding its data center capacity.
Deep-pocketed hyperscalers – Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft – don’t have that problem. But their stocks have been slammed in recent weeks as investors grow impatient with what they view as an unsustainable amount of spending that may not return profits for years.
“AI is catching a break here,” said Joe Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM US.
Brusuelas expects growth to slow from last quarter’s 3.4% pace to something closer to 2.4% if there is an AI slowdown. That’s still solid long-term growth. And America’s economy is massive and diverse. Investment that otherwise would have gone to data centers can go elsewhere.
“It’s slowing, but it doesn’t mean we’re going to have a recession,” Brusuelas said.
It also presents an opportunity for AI companies to get smart about their future AI data center rollouts – and get put on a more sustainable course.
The helter-skelter approach to data center construction has resulted in significant amounts of money getting flushed down the toilet in unworkable projects – collateral damage from massive competition to be first and biggest. Data centers already face $200 billion in project delays, according to Mike Mathews, global digital infrastructure practice leader at risk adviser Marsh.
A more rational, politically sensitive approach could create longer-term benefits for the communities that host the data centers and for the AI companies themselves.
There’s precedent for that. In the previous decade, the Googles of the world built out data centers for the cloud computing revolution, promoting the fact that they’d be built sustainably with renewable energy – even before it was cost-effective to do that. A similar, community-based approach could provide AI companies with the compute they need and give them the political and social license to operate their data centers for the long haul.
“Like the saying goes: If you want to go fast, you go it alone; if you want to go far you go together,” said Krejsa. “If you squander political license to operate at home, that’ll be a bigger impediment to remaining competitive with China.”

articles.title_orig: CVS announces major breakup, pharmacy expert weighs impact on consumers
articles.title_zh: CVS announces major breakup, pharmacy expert weighs impact on consumers
articles.content_orig:
In an interview with Fox News Digital, Douglas Hoey of the National Community Pharmacists Association said splitting CVS Pharmacy from its insurance and Pharmacy Benefits Manager businesses could improve competition and lower costs.
CVS Health on Wednesday announced plans to split its sprawling conglomerate into separate health insurance and pharmacy businesses, a move one industry expert welcomed as a potential way to drive down costs for millions of Americans.
The separation is expected to be completed by the first half of 2028, creating two independent, publicly traded companies.
The healthcare solutions company, which will temporarily retain the CVS Health name, will include its pharmacy benefit manager (PBM) insurance plans and subsidiaries, including Aetna, CVS Caremark, CVS Specialty, Oak Street Health and Signify Health.
CVS Pharmacy, the company's retail division, will include roughly 9,000 stores, its mail-order pharmacy business, MinuteClinic and the Health100 technology services unit.
CVS PHARMACY REACHES $315M SETTLEMENT WITH JUSTICE DEPARTMENT OVER CONTROLLED SUBSTANCE PRESCRIPTIONS
CVS Pharmacy, the company's retail division, will include roughly 9,000 stores. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images, File / Getty Images)
Existing CVS Health investors will receive shares in both companies tax-free, according to the Woonsocket, Rhode Island-based company.
The announcement rattled investors, sending CVS shares plunging nearly 13% Wednesday to levels not seen since spring.
For independent pharmacies, however, the breakup could create a more level playing field against the retail pharmacy giant.
An industry expert representing thousands of independent pharmacies told FOX Business that the move could restore market competition, improve patient access to medications and potentially lower prescription drug costs if "CVS becomes a true partner with other pharmacies."
"We think it will be good for competition, good for patients, lower prices, good for small businesses to be able to compete against these conglomerates," Douglas Hoey of the National Community Pharmacists Association (NCPA) said.
CVS OFFERS NEW PHARMACY OPTION FOR PET OWNERS
A customer stands at the drop-off counter inside a CVS Pharmacy store. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images, File / Getty Images)
As a standalone entity, the CVS retail pharmacy business could see more store closures, Hoey added, pointing to the company's track record of shuttering roughly 10% of its locations over the past five years due to underperformance.
"With the company split off to be a CVS Pharmacy, my guess would be that they're going to look even more closely at underperforming stores and want to close underperforming stores," Hoey said. "The good news for patients is that most of the time.
"CVSs are located near other pharmacies … And so when one closes, there's usually another option, whether it's an independent or another chain that patients can choose from."
Hoey added that the separation could help level the playing field in the pharmacy market, arguing that CVS's competitive practices have contributed to the closure of independent pharmacies. Today, he said, only about one-third of pharmacies nationwide are independently owned.
FTC TO INVESTIGATE CVS CAREMARK, HUMANA, OTHER PHARMACY BENEFIT MANAGERS
A CVS MinuteClinic patient exam room in South Portland, Me. (Gabe Souza/Portland Press Herald via Getty Images, File / Getty Images)
"Independent pharmacies have gone out of business. Rite Aid has declared bankruptcy. Walgreens is no longer a publicly traded company. They were taken off the stock market because they were purchased by private equity," Hoey said.
"CVS is not only a competitor, but they decide how much their competition gets paid. They can also decide where patients can go to get their medicine ," Hoey said.
Splitting the company would mean that CVS would not be deciding "who's the judge, the jury and the executioner for all the other pharmacies?" Hoey said.
CVS may have pursued the separation for two primary reasons, Hoey said.
The move could unlock shareholder value by separating its slower-growing, lower-margin retail drugstore business from its faster-growing, more profitable healthcare divisions .
In a statement released Tuesday, CVS said the restructuring would allow the company to "evolve into two companies with greater focus and more value for stakeholders."
A CVS pharmacist prepares vaccinations at a store in Huntington Park, Calif. (Christina House / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images, File / Getty Images)
Hoey added that the split could also help the company get ahead of mounting regulatory scrutiny over vertical integration, which allows companies to steer patients, dictate drug coverage, and underpay competing pharmacies.
In 2025 and 2026, Arkansas and Tennessee, for example, passed laws barring PBMs from owning retail pharmacies, citing potential conflicts of interest. Both measures, however, are facing ongoing federal legal challenges.
"CVS decides how much other pharmacies get paid. They also decide where patients can go to get their prescriptions," Hoey said.
"In some instances, they pay themselves more than they pay other pharmacies."
However, in its legal challenge to Tennessee's law, CVS argued that PBMs operating in the state already comply with existing requirements that they "reimburse nonaffiliated pharmacies at the same or higher rate than affiliated pharmacies, and it prohibits PBMs from steering patients to affiliated pharmacies rather than nonaffiliated pharmacies."
As a standalone entity, the CVS retail pharmacy business could see more store closures, Hoey says. ( Paul Weaver/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images, File / Getty Images)
The NCPA added that while the split is a positive development, investors will continue to hold stocks in both companies, potentially giving shareholders an incentive to see the two businesses favor one another.
"We need more information as to how they're going to be regulated," Hoey said.
Additionally, CVS Specialty will remain under the company's healthcare solutions division rather than its pharmacy business.
Hoey said that means its highly lucrative specialty mail-order operations, which handle high-cost medications for cancer, multiple sclerosis and rheumatoid arthritis, as well as GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic, will remain part of the PBM and insurance business.
CLICK HERE TO GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO
As a result, potential conflicts of interest involving patient steering and drug rebate arrangements could remain a concern in the specialty medication market.
"They should behave like a regular pharmacy, but we'll see how that goes. We need more information as to how they're going to be regulated," Hoey said.
CVS did not immediately respond to FOX Business' request for comment.

articles.title_orig: Arab parties extend a hand to try to topple Netanyahu but challenges remain
articles.title_zh: Arab parties extend a hand to try to topple Netanyahu but challenges remain
articles.content_orig:
Netanyahu: letting Arab parties into gov’t will ‘dismantle’ Israel
Israel’s President Isaac Herzog has accepted the certified results of last week’s parliamentary elections and begun consultations with party leaders on whom to task with forming the next government.
The moves on Wednesday dealt a blow to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s efforts to discredit the vote, in which he and his allies lost their majority in the 120-member parliament, while Arab-led parties made historic gains.
“The elections are over. Now is the time to face reality,” Herzog said.
In the October 27 vote, neither Netanyahu’s coalition nor the bloc of his chief rival, opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, secured the 61 seats required to govern. The prime minister’s coalition won 53, while Eisonkot’s got 48.
That leaves open the possibility of an alliance between the two men or an alliance between Eisenkot and the Arab-led parties – Ra’am and the Joint List – which had secured a record 19 seats.
Herzog concluded the first day of consultations with party leaders on Wednesday night, and said talks would continue on Thursday.
On Wednesday, the president said he met with representatives of the Religious Zionism and Zehut, Shas, and Yisrael Beytenu factions. He “received their recommendations regarding the identity of the Knesset member upon whom the task of forming the government should be assigned,” Herzog said on X.
Three factions aligned with Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist base recommended that the prime minister be given a chance to form a coalition, while a fourth, led by a former Netanyahu ally turned rival, backed Eisenkot.
Eight more parties, including the two Arab-led factions, are scheduled to meet with the president on Thursday, with Eisenkot’s Yashar party and Netanyahu’s Likud going last.
Eisenkot’s prospects improved when Ra’am, a major Arab-led party, said it would recommend him. That brought his expected support to 56 lawmakers, according to the Israeli news site Ynet, which is still short of a majority.
The other Arab-led party, the Joint List, has not announced its position. Israel’s Channel 12 reported that the party was expected to coordinate with Eisenkot, endorsing him if asked or abstaining if he preferred. Its 11 seats could push him past 61.
Netanyahu’s 53-seat bloc, by contrast, may not yield 53 endorsements.
Degel HaTorah, which holds four of United Torah Judaism’s seven seats, said it would recommend neither candidate. The ultra-Orthodox faction broke with Netanyahu over his coalition’s failure to pass legislation exempting Haredi men from military service, The Times of Israel reported.
Once the consultations end, Herzog will choose the candidate he considers best placed to assemble a coalition, almost certainly Netanyahu or Eisenkot. He has several days to announce his decision, after which the nominee will have 28 days to form a government, with a possible 14-day extension.
If neither man succeeds, Israel would hold another election early next year.
Netanyahu and his supporters meanwhile have repeatedly made unsubstantiated claims that the Arab-led parties had “stolen” the election, possibly with foreign assistance.
But Israel’s elections commission said earlier on Wednesday that it had conducted a thorough investigation of all parties’ claims of fraud and found “no evidence of irregularities that compromised the integrity of the election or affected its results”.
Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara also rejected a request to question elected officials without supporting evidence.
Herzog urged both camps to compromise to avoid a new election, saying they must accept that “not every commitment and promise can be fulfilled”.
“In the current reality, in which there is no clear winner after the elections, I ask for originality and creativity, courage and goodwill, so that the State of Israel emerges the winner,” he said.
He also backed investigating the suspected interference but warned against smearing Palestinian-Israeli voters, saying he had “great respect” for Israel’s Palestinian minority, which makes up about 20 percent of the population.
“I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Does the blue wave mean lower gasoline and diesel prices soon? Don’t hold your breath
articles.title_zh: Does the blue wave mean lower gasoline and diesel prices soon? Don’t hold your breath
articles.content_orig:
A customer replaces the nozzle on a gasoline pump after making a purchase at Fuel City filling station Friday, April 17, 2026, in Dallas. Tony Gutierrez/AP hide caption
Sign up for the Planet Money newsletter. The world is confusing. Economics can help
Democrats are now poised to take control of Congress by wide margins — and a critical driver of their success has been voter fury about how the war in Iran has driven up the cost of fuel.
Before the war, about one fifth of the world's oil passed through the Strait of Hormuz. As the war throttled that waterway , the price of oil rose : A barrel of Brent crude cost about $70 in late February, spent months hovering around the $110 mark, and is now close to $95.
That's driven up the price of everything that's refined from crude. A gallon of gas costs $4.12 on average — about $1 higher than a year ago. The price of diesel hit a record high in September at $6.52, and while it's fallen a bit since then, a gallon remains about $2.50 higher than this time last year, according to AAA .
These soaring prices helped major oil companies rake in huge profits over the past two quarters , while making the cost of fuel at the pump uncomfortably high for drivers, and boosting the price of nearly everything in a nation that is heavily reliant on trucking .
So now that the midterm results are in, could drivers see lower gasoline and diesel prices anytime soon?
Not so fast, experts say. Here's why.
Nothing yet — members of the new Congress won't be sworn in until January.
And once they are seated, U.S. legislators have limited powers to directly affect the price of oil, which is dictated by a complex global market.
In the run-up to the election, most of the actions taken by the federal government to lower fuel prices came through the White House, not Congress. Hoping to stave off losses for his party, President Trump tried to ease the cost of diesel by loosening federal rules on dyed diesel , which is normally used for farming. He also announced a deal that would bring more Russian diesel to global markets, including the U.S., by temporarily lifting sanctions. Neither of these did much to move the needle.
But the new Congressional Democrats will have the power to push the president to end the war in Iran, in part by making it harder to authorize new war spending. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D.-NY) told reporters on Wednesday that Democrats are intent on ending the war and bringing down the cost of living, saying that "relief is on the way."
"What a unified Democratic Congress can do is make escalation considerably more costly: both chambers can pass resolutions, attach conditions to war spending and hold back confirmations of key officials," Claudio Galimberti, chief economist of Rystad Energy, wrote in a market note to the media.
Still, the president has veto power over legislation, as well as executive powers. " President Trump still retains full discretionary authority over military strikes, over blockades and sanctions, licenses, and so on," said Jorge León,  head of geopolitical analysis at Rystad Energy, in an interview with NPR.
Trump has sent mixed messages about whether he wants to end or escalate the war. In the past few weeks, he warned Gulf Arab countries to prepare for a new military campaign after the midterms. The U.S. struck Qeshm , an island in the Strait of Hormuz that Iran uses to launch its own strikes, on Nov. 2.
But on election night, Trump told The New York Times that he knew voters were unhappy about gas prices . And the next day, as the extent of the election rout became clear, Vice President JD Vance posted on social media: "The reason we lost is the war."
Jaime Brito, executive director of refining and oil markets for Dow Jones Energy, says if there's a deal to end the war, traders could be very excited. Brito said they might look for formal announcements from both Iran and the U.S. that the strait is reopening, and that both sides are pulling back their military presence in the area.
If market traders are convinced the peace will last? "If that scenario happens, then I personally see crude prices dropping, you know, $15, $20 [a barrel] immediately, in the next two, three days from the announcement," he said.
But for gasoline and diesel prices to fall, too, oil would have to start moving again. Ships that have been running long, alternative routes to avoid passing through the Strait of Hormuz would have to return to their points of origin, and then resume their former routes through the strait. León pointed out, that could lead to traffic jams.
From there, that crude will still need to be refined and make its way onto the market.
In the most optimistic scenario, Brito said, it could take three months after a ceasefire or deal is announced for gasoline and diesel prices to hit their prewar levels.
León thinks it would take more like six months for the price of crude to hit its prewar level, and then another month or two for gasoline and diesel to follow. But that's assuming all goes well. And, both of them said, there could be hiccups along the way that stretch the recovery timeline out for up to a year after a deal is announced.
" I don't want to say this, but, you know, expensive gasoline prices could be a new normal," Brito said.
The first big X factor: the war in Ukraine.
If Ukraine continues attacking Russian refineries, the price of diesel may not drop as precipitously as gasoline might. That's because Russia's refineries normally bring much of the world's diesel to global markets. Resuming traffic through the Strait of Hormuz will help lower the price of diesel — but it may take longer to reach its prewar level, León said.
Other scenarios could make for a less rosy picture, León said. U.S. refineries have been running above 90% capacity — what if they need emergency maintenance just at the moment when there's more oil ready to bring to market? Or, what if hostilities restart again, despite a deal?
Brito agreed. Before the end of the year, there could theoretically be new attacks in the strait, he wrote, "if the current administration sees it as a 'window' to complete unfinished tasks before the new Congressional layout takes their seat in January."
And there's also one more factor at play: The war has raised the price of moving oil itself around the world.
Since the Strait of Hormuz has been blocked off for so long, freight costs have gone up; ships carrying oil have had to skirt around the strait, take longer routes and use more fuel in the process. Plus, the price of insuring those ships has gone up, since transit around the strait has gotten so much riskier.
That means that even the oil industry is paying more to be in the oil business. And if hostilities persist and those freight costs remain high, that could keep the price of Brent crude elevated for longer.
"Bottom line," Brito wrote, for any hope of a return to normal prices, "you need to see a definitive end of the conflict."

articles.title_orig: Trump's Fed pressure campaign hits a new Democratic wall in the Senate
articles.title_zh: Trump's Fed pressure campaign hits a new Democratic wall in the Senate
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Democrats secured control of the Senate on Tuesday, a seismic shift that effectively blocks President Trump's campaign to reshape the Federal Reserve and neutralizes what many analysts viewed as a threat to the central bank's independence.
It also heightens the challenge for Trump should he maneuver to replace any sitting officials.
"Democrats' control of the Senate reclaims the party's ability to approve or deny the President's nominees for judges and heads of other executive branch agencies," Jonathan Pingle, an economist for UBS, wrote in a note. "That includes the need for Democrats to approve any new members of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System should one of the existing governors step aside."
That political firewall directly impacts the administration's ongoing effort to remove Fed governor Lisa Cook. Trump fired Cook in August 2025, claiming she committed mortgage fraud by making misrepresentations on loan documents years before her appointment to the central bank. Cook, a Biden appointee, has denied any wrongdoing and sued. The lawsuit has gone through multiple court rungs before reaching the Supreme Court earlier this year.
Last month, Trump established a committee to determine whether her statements constituted legal "cause" for removal from the central bank, signaling that his efforts to oust her are continuing.
Read more: How much control does the president have over the Fed and interest rates?
However, Tuesday's election significantly changed the stakes of that investigation. Michael Feroli, chief US economist for JPMorgan, noted that the Senate flip alters the math for the White House.
"Even a successful removal would not open a seat up to a friend of the administration," Feroli wrote in a client note.
Jaret Seiberg, analyst with TD Cowen, agreed that the inability to confirm a replacement may make Trump less inclined to fire Cook.
Not everyone is convinced the administration will back down, however. Loretta Mester, former head of the Cleveland Fed, told Yahoo Finance, "Perhaps it makes it less likely he will succeed, but I'm not convinced it will stop the president from trying."
More broadly, Democrats taking power in Congress changes the atmosphere in which Fed officials work to set monetary policy devoid of political influence.
Trump has been vocal and persistent in urging policymakers to lower interest rates. The central bank has held steady, raising rates at times despite the White House pressure. The new power dynamic gives them more cover.
"The election result means the president has less leverage — on Congress, on the country and on the Fed," Daleep Singh, chief global economist at PGIM and a former senior official in the Biden administration, said in an interview on Bloomberg Television. "Voters are angry about the rising cost of living. You put those two thoughts together, and the Fed is uniquely positioned to do something about it."
Read more: How jobs, inflation, and the Fed are all related
Beyond the Cook dispute, the new Senate majority will dictate the Fed's long-term leadership.
While natural turnover on the Board of Governors for 14-year terms is historically slow, key institutional shifts are looming. There is only one governor whose term ends in the next two years — Jay Powell's in January 2028. As a result of the election, the administration will now need to replace Powell with someone amenable to Senate Democrats, or else leave the seat vacant. Vice Chair Philip Jefferson's term as vice chair ends in September, though he could remain as a governor.
In the near term, the political shift provides breathing room for current Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, Trump's hand-picked appointee.
RSM economist Joseph Brusuelas deemed Warsh one of the big winners of the election.
"One gets the sense that the administration will have other priorities over the next two years," Brusuelas wrote on X. "Warsh and the Fed will be free to pursue price stability and shaping policy in the best interests of the economy rather than the incumbent."
But Feroli warned that if Warsh wants to remain Fed chair beyond one term, which ends in May 2030, he should begin courting the new legislative majority.
"While there's another election between now and then, last night increased the odds his term will end with Democratic control of the Senate," Feroli said. "Unless he wants to be a one-term chair, Warsh will need to spend less time looking out the window and more time walking the halls of Congress."

articles.title_zh: Sudan, Ethiopia shut each other’s consulates in tit-for-tat move: Reports
articles.content_orig:
Sudan has closed Ethiopia’s consulate near their shared border and expelled its diplomats, hours after Addis Ababa expelled six Sudanese diplomats and shut down Khartoum’s consulate in the region, according to media reports.
Ethiopian and Sudanese officials told the Reuters and AFP news agencies about the tit-for-tat moves on Wednesday, as tensions continue to rise between the two countries. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity.
Sudan accuses Ethiopia of aiding the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a Sudanese paramilitary group embroiled in a civil war against the country’s regular army.
Ethiopia, meanwhile, accuses Sudan of backing rebels the government in Addis Ababa is fighting in the northern ⁠Tigray region.
The allegations and counter-allegations, which both sides deny, have raised fears that the two conflicts could bleed into each other, spawning a broader war in the Horn of Africa.
Reuters, citing a senior official, reported that Ethiopia ordered six staff members of the Sudanese consulate in the border town ⁠of Asosa to leave within 48 hours. It said the official asked not to be named so he could discuss a sensitive diplomatic matter.
The Associated Press news agency also reported the action, citing an Ethiopian intelligence official. It said a Sudanese official had corroborated the expulsions, adding that Ethiopian authorities summoned Sudan’s ambassador on Sunday to announce the consulate’s closure.
The Sudanese official said the staff departed on Tuesday evening. The agency said neither official had provided a specific reason for the ousters.
In retaliation, Sudan’s government closed the Ethiopian consulate in the eastern city of Gadarif and expelled the diplomats working there, two Sudanese officials told Reuters on Wednesday.
An official separately told AFP that Sudan responded by “informing the staff of the Ethiopian consulate in Gadarif”, near the border, “that they were persona non grata, and gave them 48 hours to leave the country”.
The expulsions came after ⁠Sudan lodged a complaint against Ethiopia with both the United Nations Security Council and the African Union’s Peace and Security Council on Sunday, accusing Ethiopia of allowing the RSF to use its territory to launch deadly drone attacks against civilian infrastructure in Sudan.
“The Sudanese government remains committed to its right to defend its territory. Nevertheless, it is making ⁠every possible effort to avoid an open war with Ethiopia,” said Amjad Farid, political and foreign affairs adviser for Sudan’s Transitional Sovereign Council. The Sudanese council is the country’s internationally recognised collective head of state.
A direct military confrontation with Addis Ababa would severely strain an already exhausted Sudanese military apparatus, which is still involved in intense battles with the RSF in the southeast of the country.
Addis Ababa denies it supports the RSF in Sudan’s civil war.
The fighting between Sudan’s military and the RSF, which erupted in 2023, has since killed tens of thousands of people and displaced more than 14 million. The civil war has created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, according to the UN.
On Sunday, drone strikes on electricity substations in the northern Sudanese towns of al-Dabba and Abu Hamad knocked out power. Sudan’s government and the rights group Emergency Lawyers blamed the RSF.
The conflict has more widely disrupted electricity and water supplies and threatened essential medical services.
Ethiopia’s order on the Sudanese diplomats also follows its decision to expel 10 Eritrean diplomats and close Addis Ababa’s embassy in Eritrea on October 1. Eritrea responded by severing diplomatic ties.
Ethiopia also expelled an Egyptian diplomat last month. Relations with Cairo have long been strained over Ethiopia’s massive dam on the Blue Nile, which Egypt fears could threaten its water supplies.
Addis Ababa has accused Sudan, Egypt and Eritrea of supporting Tigrayan rebels who launched an offensive against Ethiopian government forces in September. All three countries have denied the accusations.

articles.title_orig: Palestine Action ban undermined confidence in anti-terror laws, Supreme Court told
articles.title_zh: Palestine Action ban undermined confidence in anti-terror laws, Supreme Court told
articles.content_orig:
The banning of Palestine Action has led to a "crisis in confidence" in the UK's anti-terrorism laws and triggered unprecedented civil disobedience from law-abiding protesters, the Supreme Court has been told.
Opening a major legal challenge to the group's proscription last year, lawyers for co-founder Huda Ammori said that no other protest organisation had been treated the same way.
They told the five justices that the UK's highest court had never before had to consider whether banning a group under terrorism legislation was compatible with freedom of speech and protest.
Twenty-seven protesters were arrested outside the Supreme Court on Wednesday as the hearing took place, the Metropolitan Police said.
Lawyers for Ammori told the court that thousands of elderly people, many veterans of other radical causes, had been arrested for holding up signs supportive of the group since its proscription.
Home Office figures seen by the BBC indicate that there have been more than 4,000 arrests so far at protests in which people have held up signs supportive of the group.
In practice, many demonstrators have been arrested more than once, with 1,200 charges authorised by prosecutors to date. Those trials are in limbo until the outcome of this case.
Henry Blaxland KC told the court that "far from depriving Palestine Action of the oxygen of publicity" and "far from discrediting its brand", proscription of the group has had the opposite effect.
"All it's done is to pour fuel on to a fire of one of the most publicly-contested issues of our time," he said.
"It was disproportionate to do that and in my submission completely unnecessary."
During often tense exchanges with the judges, Ammori's team accepted that Palestine Action could not be described as an ordinary and peaceful protest group.
They said that its members had carried out "direct action" protests by occupying or vandalising firms linked to Israel's military - with only three of 385 incidents assessed by the Home Secretary as constituting an offence under the Terrorism Act.
The UK's definition of terrorism includes incidents of serious damage to property for a cause - and at least two break-ins at defence firms have been described in criminal courts as having caused millions in damage.
Raza Husain KC, for Ammori, said that the judges had to put aside allegations of criminality - for which the state had many powers - and consider whether the Home Secretary's decision to label the group as terrorists had been disproportionate.
"Palestine Action was proscribed on the basis of less than one per cent of its actions over five years assessed as falling within the outer limits of a definition of terrorism," he said.
"The Home Secretary's own experts confirmed the vast majority of its direct action would not constitute an act of terrorism on the basis that any damage to property is typically more minor. Common tactics include graffiti, petty vandalism, occupation, and lock-ons."
One Palestine Action member has been convicted and jailed of fracturing a police officer's back with a sledgehammer - but the court was told that the group had never advocated such violence.
The Supreme Court has received arguments from free speech campaigners, arguing the ban interferes with the right to protest.
But another submission from a coalition of Jewish groups argued that Palestine Action was a "sinister" organisation intent on attacking its community interests.
"The Court of Appeal [following earlier hearings] rightly concluded that PA is a violent organisation concerned in terrorism with a wide range of targets," said Adam Wagner KC in written submissions for the Jewish communal groups.
He continued: "Its activities are often undertaken covertly with no suggestion of restraint or proportionality, and that at the point it was proscribed it had an escalating trajectory of seriousness and an expanding focus."
Wagner said Palestine Action's "crosshairs" had moved from targeting Elbit, a defence firm with an Israeli parent company, to "figures or institutions deemed by PA to be 'Zionist'".
"Because most British Jews and Jewish institutions have a connection with Israel, a campaign against institutions PA's activists consider to be 'complicit' with Israel is, in practice, a campaign that threatens the mainstream Jewish community," he said.
However, Jewish Bloc, a group that campaigns in solidarity with Palestinians, told has also written to the court to say that claims that PA targeted their community were a "fundamental misrepresentation of the underlying evidence".
Rachel Scott KC, for the organisation, told the justices: "Neither the Jewish Leadership Council (JLC) nor the Community Security Trust (CST) have any democratic mandate. Claims that either organisation can be viewed as the voice of British Jews must therefore be viewed with very significant caution.
"The framing of PA as an organisation which threatened and intimidated 'the Jewish Community' is demonstrably false and a deliberate elision. The evidence instead shows that it targeted entities, organisations and institutions  with an established link to Israel's illegal activities against the Palestinian people."
The case continues on Thursday with a judgment expected at a later date.

articles.title_orig: Israel’s Herzog accepts vote results, opens talks on forming a government
articles.title_zh: Israel’s Herzog accepts vote results, opens talks on forming a government
articles.content_orig:
Netanyahu: letting Arab parties into gov’t will ‘dismantle’ Israel
Israel’s President Isaac Herzog has accepted the certified results of last week’s parliamentary elections and begun consultations with party leaders on whom to task with forming the next government.
The moves on Wednesday dealt a blow to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s efforts to discredit the vote, in which he and his allies lost their majority in the 120-member parliament, while Arab-led parties made historic gains.
“The elections are over. Now is the time to face reality,” Herzog said.
In the October 27 vote, neither Netanyahu’s coalition nor the bloc of his chief rival, opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, secured the 61 seats required to govern. The prime minister’s coalition won 53, while Eisonkot’s got 48.
That leaves open the possibility of an alliance between the two men or an alliance between Eisenkot and the Arab-led parties – Ra’am and the Joint List – which had secured a record 19 seats.
Herzog concluded the first day of consultations with party leaders on Wednesday night, and said talks would continue on Thursday.
On Wednesday, the president said he met with representatives of the Religious Zionism and Zehut, Shas, and Yisrael Beytenu factions. He “received their recommendations regarding the identity of the Knesset member upon whom the task of forming the government should be assigned,” Herzog said on X.
Three factions aligned with Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist base recommended that the prime minister be given a chance to form a coalition, while a fourth, led by a former Netanyahu ally turned rival, backed Eisenkot.
Eight more parties, including the two Arab-led factions, are scheduled to meet with the president on Thursday, with Eisenkot’s Yashar party and Netanyahu’s Likud going last.
Eisenkot’s prospects improved when Ra’am, a major Arab-led party, said it would recommend him. That brought his expected support to 56 lawmakers, according to the Israeli news site Ynet, which is still short of a majority.
The other Arab-led party, the Joint List, has not announced its position. Israel’s Channel 12 reported that the party was expected to coordinate with Eisenkot, endorsing him if asked or abstaining if he preferred. Its 11 seats could push him past 61.
Netanyahu’s 53-seat bloc, by contrast, may not yield 53 endorsements.
Degel HaTorah, which holds four of United Torah Judaism’s seven seats, said it would recommend neither candidate. The ultra-Orthodox faction broke with Netanyahu over his coalition’s failure to pass legislation exempting Haredi men from military service, The Times of Israel reported.
Once the consultations end, Herzog will choose the candidate he considers best placed to assemble a coalition, almost certainly Netanyahu or Eisenkot. He has several days to announce his decision, after which the nominee will have 28 days to form a government, with a possible 14-day extension.
If neither man succeeds, Israel would hold another election early next year.
Netanyahu and his supporters meanwhile have repeatedly made unsubstantiated claims that the Arab-led parties had “stolen” the election, possibly with foreign assistance.
But Israel’s elections commission said earlier on Wednesday that it had conducted a thorough investigation of all parties’ claims of fraud and found “no evidence of irregularities that compromised the integrity of the election or affected its results”.
Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara also rejected a request to question elected officials without supporting evidence.
Herzog urged both camps to compromise to avoid a new election, saying they must accept that “not every commitment and promise can be fulfilled”.
“In the current reality, in which there is no clear winner after the elections, I ask for originality and creativity, courage and goodwill, so that the State of Israel emerges the winner,” he said.
He also backed investigating the suspected interference but warned against smearing Palestinian-Israeli voters, saying he had “great respect” for Israel’s Palestinian minority, which makes up about 20 percent of the population.
“I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Altar Stone mystery continues as theory overturned
articles.title_zh: Altar Stone mystery continues as theory overturned
articles.content_orig:
A new study exploring the origins of the six tonne Altar Stone at Stonehenge has ruled out a theory that it came from an area of Scotland.
The 4.9 metre sandstone slab within the circle was initially believed to have originated in Wales until a more recent study pointed towards it coming from north east Scotland.
Scientific tests were carried out in the Orcadian Basin area of Scotland, but researchers failed to find a location with the same characteristics of the stone in that area.
However study lead, Professor Duncan Pirrie from the University of South Wales, said the latest investigation has left them "far better equipped to focus on the areas most likely to yield an answer."
Pirrie said his latest publication on the Altar Stone has "built the clearest picture yet" and was "the most comprehensive geological investigation of the Altar Stone ever undertaken".
Professor Nick Pearce from Aberystwyth University, who worked on the previous research, said "ruling out potential source areas is just as important as identifying new ones".
The geochemistry expert said: "Every location eliminated narrows the search and brings us closer to discovering where the Altar Stone originated.
"The stone is unique among those at Stonehenge, and tracing its source would provide valuable new insights into its remarkable journey to Salisbury Plain thousands of years ago."
The world-famous Wiltshire monument was constructed in multiple phases over thousands of years, between 3000 and 1600 BC. However, not all stones come from the area.
The smaller bluestones travelled around 225km from west Wales with research suggesting a few were taken directly from another circle.
The latest study combined new observations and looked at fragments of the stone in museum collections, examining structure, minerals and composition.
It has been published in the Journal of the Geological Society.

articles.title_zh: Live: France braces for nationwide strikes in fresh test for Macron’s policies
articles.content_orig:
Hospital workers, air traffic and rail staff expected to join strikes amid renewed protests over education and rising living costs
Hundreds of thousands are expected to march in demonstrations across France as trade unions call for a nationwide strike expected to extend to hospital workers, air traffic control, the post office, teachers and rail staff.
President Emmanuel Macron’s final months in office continue to be marred by domestic crises, as high school students protesting over poor teaching conditions have been joined by workers in weekly protests over the cost of living. Meanwhile, the government is struggling to pass a belt-tightening budget in a divided parliament as public debt approaches 120% of economic output.
Ahead of Thursday’s strike action, France’s four main rail unions said that the government’s proposed budget cuts would “worsen poverty, slash social security, freeze state workers’ salaries and dry up investment needed for environmental measures”.
Amid the renewed protests centred on living costs, public spending cuts and the troubled education system, the far-right, anti-immigration candidate Marine Le Pen is polling high for the 2027 presidential election to replace Macron next spring.
High school students continued to blockade schools over overcrowded classes and dilapidated buildings, saying the government’s proposed measures on capping some class sizes and loaning funds to regional authorities to fix schools were not enough. University students joined in blockading some faculties. Trade unions from across the political landscape joined in a call for strikes over the rising cost of living, with private schools’ teachers unions also joining strikes alongside state school teachers.
Rights’ groups protested over what they said was heavy policing and an “authoritarian” attempt by Macron’s executive to clamp down on the right to demonstrate.
The French Human Rights League said there was an “authoritarian shift” to stifle “any dissenting voice” as the government put in place heavy policing and authorities issued restrictions on demonstrating in city centres, as well as curfews in certain areas.
Sophie Binet, the head of the leftwing CGT union, said: “We’re living at a very serious time with a very dangerous authoritarian drift from the government”, criticising decisions by authorities in cities such as Rennes, Toulouse and Lyon to push demonstrations out of city centres.
